:::{#def-eigendecomposition}
#### Eigendecomposition

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ symmetric matrix with real entries.
An **eigendecomposition**, or **spectral decomposition**, of $\matr{A}$
is a factorization

$$
\matr{A} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}
$$

with $\matr{Q}$ a $p \times p$ orthogonal matrix (@def-orthogonal-matrix)
and $\matr{\Lambda}$ a $p \times p$ diagonal matrix (@def-diagonal-matrix).
@thm-spectral says that every such $\matr{A}$ has one.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-spectral}
#### An eigendecomposition of a $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$,
@exm-eigenvalue found the eigenvectors $(1, 1)$ for $3$ and $(1, -1)$ for $1$.
They are orthogonal (@def-orthogonal-vectors):

$$
\ba
(1, 1) \cdot (1, -1)
&= 1 \cd 1 + 1 \cd (-1)
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= 1 - 1
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 0
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

Each has norm $\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}$ (@def-euclidean-norm),
so dividing each by $\sqrt{2}$ gives two orthonormal eigenvectors
(@def-orthonormal-vectors).
Put them in the columns of $\matr{Q}$,
and the matching eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\matr{\Lambda}$:

$$
\matr{Q} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

This $\matr{Q}$ is symmetric, so $\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{Q}$. Then

$$
\ba
\matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cd \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(move the scalars to the front)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply the scalars)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \cd 3 + 1 \cd 0 & 1 \cd 0 + 1 \cd 1 \\ 1 \cd 3 + (-1) \cd 0 & 1 \cd 0 + (-1) \cd 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication, first two matrices)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 + 0 & 0 + 1 \\ 3 + 0 & 0 - 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 \cd 1 + 1 \cd 1 & 3 \cd 1 + 1 \cd (-1) \\ 3 \cd 1 + (-1) \cd 1 & 3 \cd 1 + (-1) \cd (-1) \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 + 1 & 3 - 1 \\ 3 - 1 & 3 + 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply by } \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

which is $\matr{A}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-eigendecomposition-not-unique}
#### An eigendecomposition is not unique

A symmetric matrix can have more than one eigendecomposition.
Reordering the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\matr{\Lambda}$,
and the columns of $\matr{Q}$ with them, gives another one,
and so does multiplying a column of $\matr{Q}$ by $-1$.

For example, take $\matr{A}$ from @exm-spectral.
Swapping the two eigenvalues and the two columns gives

$$
\matr{Q}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{\Lambda}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

and multiplying the second column of $\matr{Q}$ by $-1$ gives

$$
\matr{Q}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{\Lambda}_2 = \matr{\Lambda} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The columns of $\matr{Q}_1$ and $\matr{Q}_2$
are the columns of $\matr{Q}$, reordered or multiplied by $-1$,
so they are still orthonormal,
and $\matr{Q}_1$ and $\matr{Q}_2$ are orthogonal.
Both products give back $\matr{A}$:

$$
\ba
\matr{Q}_1\matr{\Lambda}_1\tp{\matr{Q}_1}
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute; multiply the scalars)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply the first two matrices)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 + 3 & -1 + 3 \\ -1 + 3 & 1 + 3 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add; multiply by } \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

$$
\ba
\matr{Q}_2\matr{\Lambda}_2\tp{\matr{Q}_2}
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute; multiply the scalars)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply the first two matrices)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\begin{bmatrix} 3 + 1 & 3 - 1 \\ 3 - 1 & 3 + 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add; multiply by } \tfrac{1}{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::
